sets.pad: Cape Canaveral launch pad at night, Nov 2025. far: SpaceBackdrop #080614 with stars; mid: pale-rimmed launch tower silhouette and a tall dark rocket with a warm Glow at the base; near: GroundPlane of dark concrete with pale rim and two floodlights with bloom. setp.fire 0..1 = engine plume size and sparks; at 1 the rocket rises with a long flame. setp.tint 'night' (default) | 'dawn'.
sets.sunside: Solar-system diagram, top view. Sun glow at centre (gold, big bloom), thin dashed cream orbit rings for Earth (inner) and Mars (outer), Earth as small blue-green disc, Mars as small red disc. setp.view 'opposite' = Earth and Mars on opposite sides of the Sun with a dashed line through the Sun and a red X on the line; 'aligned' = Earth and Mars close together on the same side with a green tick; 'flight' = a teal curved flight arc from Earth to Mars. setp.t 0..1 animates the planets or craft along the path.
sets.loiter: Close diagram of Earth and the L2 point. Earth as a blue-green disc at left with pale rim, the Sun far off-left as a faint glow, a small gold-dotted L2 marker about a million miles to the right of Earth, and a kidney-bean-shaped teal looping path around L2 with a small twin-craft dot travelling along it. setp.t 0..1 = position along the loop (0 start near Earth, 0.5 far side of L2, 1 back at Earth). setp.zoom 0..1 pushes in.
sets.flyby: Earth close-up from space. A huge curved Earth limb (deep blue disc, pale rim, thin cyan atmosphere band) filling the bottom, stars above. A small twin-spacecraft silhouette passes left to right with a teal trail. setp.t 0..1 = craft position along the pass; setp.burn 0..1 draws an orange glowing arc along the trail (the engine burn) growing with burn; setp.alt shows a thin dashed altitude line from the craft down to the limb.
sets.ops: Mission operations room, UC Berkeley style. far: wall of dark screens showing glowing cream trajectory curves; mid: two rows of desks with dark monitors, tiny warm lamp glows, no faces; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim. setp.tension 0..1 = number of screens flashing amber; setp.ok 1 turns all screens green with a soft pulse.
sets.mars: Mars close-up. A big red-orange Mars disc with simple outlined darker patches, pale rim, thin faint atmosphere glow, stars behind. setp.orbit 0..1 = a dashed teal orbit ring around Mars with a small craft dot travelling it; setp.wind 0..1 = number of pale-yellow solar-wind particles streaming from the left and bending around the planet, some stripping away from the top as a thin ghost tail.
sets.cruise: Transfer-orbit diagram. Sun glow left-centre, Earth orbit ring, Mars orbit ring, and a teal curved arc from Earth to Mars with a small twin-craft dot. setp.t 0..1 travel along the arc; setp.months shows a small month ticker on the arc.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in minutes: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.calendar: Wall calendar card, cream page, 4 px dark outline, big text from pp.year (a year number or a short word like NOV 7) in FONTS.title; page flips once when p passes 0.3 if pp.flip.
props.probe: Small twin-spacecraft icon: two teal-and-cream boxy craft side by side with dark outline, gold solar-panel wings, tiny antenna, soft rim light; pp.glow true adds an orange engine glow behind; pp.s scale.
props.earth: Small Earth disc, blue-green with simple outlined continents, pale rim, subtle atmosphere glow. pp.tilt degrees.
props.marsdisc: Small Mars disc, red-orange with dark outlined patches, pale rim and bloom; pp.s scale.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.stopwatch: Round outlined stopwatch, cream face, red button on top; pp.from..pp.to minutes: hand sweeps and digits count.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.thermos: Mustard thermos flask with a dark cap and a little steam curl (Glow).
props.sign: Hand-painted sign on a post, cream board, dark outline, pp.text in FONTS.hand (max 12 chars).

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: Six hundred fifty miles up.
Engine on.
For nine minutes.
And Earth throws you at Mars.
No rocket big enough. Just a planet's pull.
NASA did it twice. In two days.
So what if you were riding along?
What if Earth were your slingshot?
Here are the rules.
You are one of two small spacecraft.
Your target is Mars.
You cannot just point and go.
You need Earth to do the heavy lifting.
And you have one shot at it.
Miss the window, and Mars waits two years.
Or does it?
November thirteenth, twenty twenty-five.
You lift off from Cape Canaveral.
A perfect launch.
There is just one problem.
Earth and Mars are on opposite sides of the Sun.
Wrong side. Wrong time.
A direct flight would take forever.
So you do something clever.
You do not head for Mars at all.
You head for a spot in space, near home.
It sits about a million miles from Earth.
Straight away from the Sun.
Scientists call it Lagrange point two.
A gravitational balancing point.
Nothing pulls you in. Nothing pushes you out.
So you drift. In a loop.
A kidney-bean-shaped loop, to be exact.
The first of its kind.
You are parked. You are not stuck.
And Earth is still close enough to find.
Now you wait.
A whole year, going in circles.
No sightseeing. Just loops.
You do take a few measurements.
Out here, you fly through Earth's long magnetic tail.
The solar wind stretches it out like a windsock.
Then, one day, the timing is right.
Mars has moved to the same side of the Sun as Earth.
So you turn around and head home.
Not to land. To skim past.
November seventh, twenty twenty-six.
Mission control holds its breath.
At five in the morning, Eastern time, you arrive.
One thousand miles above the ground.
Close enough to feel Earth's pull.
Now the engine fires.
This is the burn that commits you.
Trans-Mars injection, they call it.
Nine minutes of thrust.
Earth's gravity bends your path.
The engine adds a push, right where gravity is strongest.
Two forces, working as one.
And then the thrust ends.
You are on your way to Mars.
Mission control erupts.
Nobody at NASA had ever done this before.
But remember, you are one of two.
Your twin is still coming round.
Two days later, same plan.
Monday, around six in the morning, Eastern.
This time, even closer.
Six hundred fifty miles up.
Another nine-minute burn.
Flawless again.
Two spacecraft. Two flybys. Two days.
A new way to reach Mars.
You can launch almost any time.
Then park, wait, and slingshot.
No more waiting for the planets to line up every two years.
Now comes the quiet part.
Ten months of coasting.
No engine. No drama. Just falling toward Mars.
You still work on the way.
The solar wind is changing between here and Mars.
A stream of particles, a million miles an hour.
A few small nudges keep you on course.
Each one has to be precise.
Because Mars will not wait.
September seventh, twenty twenty-seven.
Mars fills the window.
Now you have to slow down.
Another burn. About eleven minutes.
Get it wrong, and you sail straight past.
Get it right, and Mars catches you.
Your twin does the same, two days later.
Two small craft, circling the Red Planet.
Then the real work begins.
Science starts around June twenty twenty-eight.
So what is the mission actually for?
Mars used to have a thick atmosphere.
The solar wind may have stripped it away.
Two spacecraft, in two places, at once.
One out near the wind. One close to the planet.
Watching Mars respond in real time.
That helps us plan for the first humans there.
So back to that moment.
Engine on. Nine minutes. Earth's pull.
And a planet you have never visited.
Earth gave you a push. Mars is next.
Would you have taken the slingshot?
Tomorrow: another what if, another piece of the sky.

short.vo: Six hundred fifty miles up. Engine on.
Nine minutes later, Earth throws you at Mars.
NASA's twin ESCAPADE probes just did it. Twice.
They launched in November twenty twenty-five.
But Mars was on the far side of the Sun.
So they parked a million miles away.
Looping in a kidney-bean path for a year.
Then Earth and Mars lined up.
One burn. Gravity does the rest.
First time NASA has done it.
Then another burn, eleven minutes, to catch Mars.
The goal: see how the solar wind strips Mars.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: another what if.
Six hundred fifty miles. Engine on.
